utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, good morning to you as well. I would like to remind you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Mikulicic, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Today we will continue where we stopped yesterday. Let us just recall that yesterday we stopped while talking about the period of the Bihac crisis and the situation when there was a threat that the Bihac enclave and the UN security zone might fall, in the military sense of the word, and numerous letters were sent at the time and we saw your last letter of the 20th of July which you sent to Mr. Blanco, who was, at the time, the president of the UN Security Council. The international public was interested in the issue of Bihac and these events. And I will show you the thoughts of Mr. Galbraith, and I will ask you whether, in context with Mr. Galbraith, you reached similar conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we please see the document D1791 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're become in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Now you may proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Granic, it's the document under tab 14 in your binder. Do you remember President Tudjman's message of the 4th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: President Tudjman said that since all attempts for a peaceful reintegration have failed from both the Croatian authorities and the international community, including yesterday's talks in Geneva, and the Croatian state is forced to take military and police measures after four years of negotiations that yielded no results. And on the second page, President Tudjman, on behalf of the democratic authorities of Croatia, called upon members of Serbian paramilitary units who were mobilised of their own free will, or forcibly, to surrender their weapons to Croatian authority with the guarantee that they will be given amnesty according to valid Croatian laws. Mr. Granic, did the state leadership discuss how the Croatian state would treat Croatian citizens in the occupied territories who were of Serbian ethnicity at the time and what would be the policy towards them?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of this was discussed a lot, including the treatment of Croatian citizens of Serbian ethnicity and the relation of the international community to this. I remember very well a discussion from early June when our primary goal was peaceful reintegration, if that was possible. That was a conversation with President Tudjman and Minister Susak. And considering the experiences from Operation Flash when a great number of the citizens of Serbian ethnicity had left the area with the assistance of the UNHCR and ICRC, that our main goal, if there was a military operation, was simply to reach the borders of Croatia and that it was in our interest to have as many of Croatian Serbs who had rebelled to remain in the area except those who had committed war crimes, of course, or those who did not wish to recognise Croatia in any form as a state. We discussed all that, and we were aware of the strong indoctrination through the media and the policy conducted from Belgrade in the previous years, at least since 1987. We were also aware that there had been plans for evacuation of citizens of Serbian ethnicity, and we were aware that many of them did not wish to accept Croatia as a state. And we were also aware that many of them had committed crimes, because during the war almost 14.000 people were killed and 36.000 wounded. We knew all this. However, we reached an agreement, and President Tudjman decided, that once again we would invite everyone who wished to stay to stay there, and so he addressed this letter to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Before that letter, as President Tudjman said himself, the negotiations fell through on the previous day, that is to say the 3rd of August, 1995, in Geneva. In a few sentences, could you please tell us what it was about?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the circumstances of an acute threat to the UN protected area in Bihac, under the circumstances in which the rebelled Serbs received additional assistance from Belgrade and were amassing weapons further, it was only clear that the plan for peaceful reintegration was made even harder. Had the plan been proposed by Mr. Stoltenberg six months before that, Croatia would have accepted it. But at that point in time, it provided nothing save for the opportunity to the Serbs to conquer Bihac. That is why we could not accept it. We knew through our permanent communication with the US - and I personally communicated with the state secretary Mr. Christopher and the US representative with the UN Ms. Madeleine Albright as well as Mr. Holbrooke, especially Mr. Holbrooke, who was the special envoy of Mr. Clinton, as well as through my contacts with the leading European prime ministers - I was aware of what the reaction would be, the reaction of the world, if we followed certain principles, primarily the protection of UNCRO, protection of civilians, as well as honouring the laws of war and international conventions. And there was one other precondition, and that was that we had to act swiftly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav public, as well as the Krajina Serb and parts of the international public, tried to speculate with the role of Milan Babic in those events, because he, at the very last moment, agreed to peaceful reintegration and peace talks. Can you tell us, actually, what the role of Milan Babic was in the negotiations and what was his importance and influence?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an attempt by Mr. Galbraith, US ambassador, to have an arrangement with Mr. Babic so that he would be forced to sit at the table and negotiate. Mr. Babic, at that point in time, had no influence whatsoever over the rebelled Serbs. The only real influence was exercised by Mr. Milan Martic. And together with Karadzic, he was embarking upon the creation of a joint state, and they were attacking Bihac together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was Babic's formal role in the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while, Babic was their prime minister. However, he moved to Belgrade, and, as of that time, he had absolutely no influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the military operation Storm ensued, whereupon you assembled the diplomatic corps representatives in Zagreb, and you explained to them the model, the motives behind the operation, as well as its results.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a meeting of the National Security Council on the 3rd of August at 6.00 p.m. We agreed that after the meeting, when the president made the official decision Operation Storm, to notify the ambassadors of the US, France, the UK, of the Russian Federation, and the Vatican. I personally travelled to Split to inform the French Foreign Minister, Mr. Juppe, at the Split airport. I think it was around 9.00 p.m. That was the time when we were supposed to inform them officially on our decision to launch the police and military operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Presiding Judge, I seek to tender 3D00466 as evidence. The president's letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1809.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1809 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This Chamber already saw evidence on the development of the operation which took four days to complete. The Serb population evacuated, and after Operation Storm, certain reactions arrived from the international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Just to be careful in characterizing. I don't know whether he's quoting the witness when he talks about the Serb population evacuated. Of course that's a highly disputed point in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I could rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the departure of the Serb citizens from the territory of the former so-called Serb Republic of Krajina, there were international reactions. Can you describe to us what sort of reactions those were and what was the general atmosphere?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initial reaction came from the co-chairperson of the conference for the former Yugoslavia, Mr. Carl Bildt. He stated that the shelling of Knin was excessive and random and that President Tudjman should stand trial for that before the International Tribunal in The Hague, that is to say, this Tribunal. Personally, as the minister, I had difficulty accepting this, because after consultations with the leading generals, Mr. Miljevac and General Cervenko, I received information that there was no excessive or random shelling which lasted for two mornings before Knin was liberated. I was told that the operation was conducted by our best generals, Mr. Gotovina and Markac, as well as the Special Police. After having consulted those who were officially in charge of the operation at the headquarters, the persons being General Miljevac and General Cervenko, I sent a very sharp note. And I was also the war deputy prime minister. Today is the 18th of November, the day when Vukovar fell, when, in only one day, there were between 6 and 8.000 shells landing daily on civilian targets. It was only understandable that I was distressed because of that, because I was aware of the high morale level of the people involved in it, and I was convinced that they would not target civilians intentionally. I went to Knin together with Mr. Tudjman at a later date. I can't say that I saw all of it, but on route between the football pitch where the helicopter had landed to the place where we had a meeting and lunch at the fortress, I basically did not see a single destroyed house. That was the reason why I reacted so strongly to Mr. Bildt's letter. Secondly, there were pressures exerted concerning the departure of Croatian Serbs. The figures presented varies; many were exaggerated. It is true that a great deal of Croatian Serbs left. However, they left in a planned way; they were stimulated to do so by their leadership. Those who left refused to recognise Croatia as a state. Those who left had been indoctrinated. And to include, those who left simply feared revenge for their earlier taking part in certain crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You described the overall events and you described the close contacts you had with the US representatives, in particular Mr. Galbraith, who was the then US ambassador to Zagreb. I want to show you another thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I would kindly ask to move into private session for that. Could we please have document D1792.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're become in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the Registrar for P458 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, we'll see a document which was already made an exhibit, that is Mr. Galbraith's diary in which he noted on his impressions. Let us go to page 36 of the diary, which deals with the events of the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 36, please. The ERN number is 065. The date, the 7th of August. The ERN number of the page is 0649065. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, in the middle of this paragraph Mr. Galbraith says as follows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, in order to avoid whatever confusion, this is in the e-court numbering page 30 out of 76. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Galbraith says as follows: "I talked to Susak. He wants to keep going in Bosnia. He says I told Granic that they should go forward, but Zuzul got the message that perhaps they should stop. I said I could not offer an official view. However, Croatia's action was welcomed by many in Washington because of its implications for Bosnia." Further on, he says that he was interviewed by the NBC and BBC. The BBC asked if Croats were engaged in ethnic cleansing. "I said no, since ethnic cleansing is a practice organised from Belgrade and carried out by Bosnian and Croatian Serbs aimed at the systematic expulsion of a people, whether Muslim or Croat, by using murder, mass rape, violence, and terror. There's no evidence that the Croatians are systematically driving out the Serbs, although there are many reports of atrocities." Next we can move to page 32 in e-court, which refers to the 9th of August. Mr. Galbraith says as follows: "I returned to Zagreb. I found out that my ethnic cleansing comments have caused controversy in the British press with the 'Independent' saying they have exacerbated US-UK tensions on Croatia. Defence Minister Portillo had said that there was ethnic cleansing. I don't like the controversy. I am right technically, but it looks as if I am apologising for the Croats." I'm interested in the following, Mr. Granic: What was the relationship between the great powers in view of their assessment of the operation? On the one hand we had the US view as articulated by Mr. Galbraith; and on the other, the view of the UK. Did you sense any difference of opinion between those two great powers?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a difference, of course. The Croatian military and police operation Storm was strategically very important for the American peace operation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Without it, the initiative would have almost completely died out. On the other hand, it should be noted that Great Britain was in charge in Bosnia and Herzegovina until the American peace initiative was launched through Lord Owen and, once Owen, Vance-Owen, Owen-Stoltenberg plans failed, the United States of America led first to the Washington and then the Dayton Accords. In other words, undoubtedly there were certain differences, although they tried to reconcile them, and to do so to a great extent, through the work in the Contact Group, especially during the Dayton Accords. It is beyond doubt that, strategically speaking, the Operation Storm fitted fully within the American peace initiative, and we were aware of it. As for the media, the accusations coming from the British media that it involved ethnic cleansing were not only inaccurate at that point but also very damaging, because, at a later date, certain events that were indeed of criminal nature on the part of the Croatian side were recognised as such due to these accusations that were initially entirely unwarranted and false, because initially the departure of the Serb population was planned, instigated, and organised due to the actual fears felt by those who had committed crimes and who had not accepted Croatia as their country. So this media campaign was initially, by all means, counter-productive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, can you give us your comments based on your extensive diplomatic experience? There's one issue that I am not quite clear on. We saw an exhibit before - that was D1792 - and we saw the reasoning of the British ambassador to Croatia, Mr. Hewitt, who was the man in the field, if we can put it that way, who said that in the context of the departure of the Serb population this was not ethnic cleansing but an evacuation of the Serb population which was encouraged and ordered by the Republic of Serbian Krajina leadership. So this was the thinking, the reasoning, of a British diplomat in Zagreb. On the other hand, we have the reasoning of the defence minister, Mr. Portillo, who stated that it was ethnic cleansing after all. What is your interpretation of the these diametrically opposed views, i.e., the assessment made by an ambassador in the field and, on the other, an assessment made by a defence minister in London?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm not sure the witness is here to be an expert on British politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness was in the midst of the events at the time, and assessments in this field are within his field of knowledge. Whatever weight to be attached to it is still to be considered by the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, can you tell us, briefly, what your comments are on this score?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ambassador Hewitt spoke on the basis of the information he had in the field. Minister Portillo gave his comments on a strategic level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page ERN 649101 of the same document. Give me a moment and I'll find the page number in e-court. That's page 65 of Mr. Galbraith's diary, which relates to the 13th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph, Mr. Galbraith says that he saw you and that there was discussion on human rights in the Krajina, the right to return, and that one needed to be serious about Eastern Slavonija negotiations. Mr. Galbraith says that you understood the message and stressed that you did not make any statements about Krajina precisely because of your concerns over what had happened there. You said that the Croatian government would be forthcoming on human -- on humanitarian returns, family reunions, individual cases, but that en masse return would have to wait a final settlement with Serbia. Can you tell us, first of all, whether this indeed reflects your conversation with Mr. Galbraith, and, if so, what is your position with regard to the en masse return of the Serb population to Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this conversation, which is accurately depicted here, three issues emerge quite clearly. Firstly, I personally condemned crimes and the criminal conduct on the Croatian side in the aftermath of the military police operation Storm. Secondly, in that period of time we were busy discussing a peaceful reintegration of the Croatian Danube area and seeking a model for such a peaceful reintegration to be implemented. This means that in Dayton, before Bosnia-Herzegovina had been discussed, the Croatian leadership demanded that the issue of a peaceful reintegration of the Croatian Danube area be agreed upon. This was one of the -- one of many discussions that took place with Mr. Galbraith. Thirdly, when the Serb population left for Belgrade and became refugees - and do not forget that they all had -- were entitled to become citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia - that was the time when terrorist attacks were being announced against Croatia, when government in exile was being set up, and there was still a danger from -- for Croatia from the FRY. There was still instances of Croats and non-Serbs being expelled from the Republika Srpska. At that time, only individual cases of return were possible aimed at family reunions. But primarily, because of security and safety reasons, no form of en masse return was possible. An en masse return, in agreement with the High Commissioner for Refugees and the international community, was made possible in the spring of 1998 when we reached an agreement over a plan for the return of refugees. It was only then that all conditions were met for such a return. It required special treatment, and it could be done only according to a detailed plan and programme in co-operation with the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 3D00538.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, could I -- I do not know whether you have dealt with it, but the concept of family reunion is not entirely clear in this context. I don't whether you're going to deal with that or whether I could ask a clarifying question to Mr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's the perfect time to ask the clarifying questions, although there's going to be our -- one the next witnesses who will be talking especially about the family reunion and all the other matters. But I'm sure the witness is very well aware what is this term. So we could ask him, just to be informed of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, if we are talking about family reunion, are we talking about reunion with family members which had stayed in the Krajina, which remained in the Krajina, after Operation Storm; or are we also talking about families being reunited in the place where they had lived even if no family member had remained during and after Operation Storm in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're referring to the family members who stayed behind in Croatia wherever, whatever the place they were, whether it be the liberated area, Zagreb, or elsewhere. Their reunion with those who left for Belgrade or for Republika Srpska. In other words, it involved any location. And if there was such a request by a family, then the ICRC and the UNHCR interceded there. And we almost always resolved such requests by granting them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if no family member had left, if no grandmother or no husband or -- had left, could there be any family reunion? No, I say "had left." I should have said "would have remained there." So if a whole family left, there was no family reunion possible. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. That's well understood, Your Honour. If everyone left, then they came under the plan and programme of the return of refugees. The plan was developed, I was personally in charge of it, and insisted that it be made. There were large discussions going on within the Croatian government as to whether the time had come for such a plan to be made. It was the time of April of 1998. For security and psychological reasons and other reasons it was being discussed -- the time was being discussed, not whether the time was right for them to return, but whether the time was right for them to return en mass. I believe that the time had come for that, and ultimately President Tudjman backed me up and the Croatian government drafted and adopted a plan which related to the return of all refugees. All of this happened over a period of some two and a half years, which is considered to be quite a short period of time, since it was a time of reconstruction. And already for ten years now this has no longer been a political issue in Croatia; it is only an economic issue. According to the current legislation, the houses of both Serbs and Croats are being reconstructed. Clearly, the houses of the Croats were reconstructed earlier on because the Croats returned sooner. But any Serb who had left at the time is entitled to return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my understand, so if a whole family left, well, let's say on the 6th of August, there was -- they had to wait for two and a half years until plans would be developed for return? Is that correctly understood, because it was not family reunion. Is that correctly understood? So apart from whether you consider that a short period of time or long period of time, I'm mainly focusing on the factual situation. The whole family which left on the 6th of August, they could not apply, from what I understand, for family reunion. And you explained to us that there were very good reasons why, only after -- or after two and a half years, a plan was put in practice for them to return not earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's correctly understood, although there were many cases where such matters were resolved sooner. As early as in September of 1995, I'm aware of a case where 50 Serb refugees, through Mr. Dzakula who interceded on their behalf, he was the local leader of Serbs in Western Slavonia, and asked that they be allowed to return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Krajina at this moment and about nothing else. I do see that the problems may have been linked, but I'm focusing on what is primarily the subject matter of this case in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've understood that correctly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic. No, one more question: Do you know the -- how many families left, all the members and from how many families what percentage one or more persons remained? I'm talking about Serb families in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The total number of persons we were sure had left was around 140.000. As for the number of those who stayed behind, I don't know the figures. I wouldn't know if one family member stayed behind, two, or more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The reaction on the part of the international community in the wake of Operation Storm was that on several occasions the Croatian government received requests concerning the deployment of monitors of the international community to be allowed to go out into the field and see for themselves what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That respect, I would like the Registrar to call up 3D00538.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: There you will see your letter, Mr. Granic, of the 14th of February, 1996, which you sent to the headquarters of OSCE in response to their request that they dispatch a fact-finding mission to Croatia. What was the position of the Croatian government that you articulated in your letter? Were you absolutely agreed to their request to come and see for themselves what the situation in the field. So what was the position of the Croatian government with regard to the EU monitoring?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position and the position of the Croatian government was to allow the presence of all and any observers or monitors who wanted to be there. The OSCE, Ms. Elizabeth Rehn, and all the other monitors, and there were many others. The Helsinki Watch. There were a great many of them. There were various human rights committees. And all of them were allowed to monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were there any conditions imposed in the sense of restrictions on monitoring missions?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no conditions imposed. At some point in 1996, we wanted to discuss that so that we would know who was doing what, but, even then, we granted absolute freedom to anyone who wanted to monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1810.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit D1810 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask the Registry for document 3D00537.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, now we shall see a note drafted by Mr. Branko Socanac, approved by Ms. Dubravka Simonovic from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, approving the arrival the fact-finding OSCE mission to Knin. And that's tab 17A in your binder, but here we can see it, and I will just point out the main things to you. It says that in Knin Mr. Pasic, who was the government commissioner to Knin, and Marko Gojevic, who was the commander of the Knin Garrison, welcomed this delegation. They informed them about the ethnic break-up of the population in Knin before the Operation Storm and what happened after it when 420 Serbs were left there and 250 had managed to return. There was possibility for them to return. And each day they received four to five requests for return, and only in one day the office for displaced persons and refugees had issued 17 return permits because of joining families. Further on it is stated that the importance of the project Save the Life was stressed when taking care of persons who had been left behind in newly liberated territories and that there were prosecutions before relevant courts. Mr. Granic, there were problems with events after the Operation Storm. There was an escalation of crimes such as looting, house burning, even murders. What was the political reaction, the reaction of the Croatian state and President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were deeply concerned about these events. In the beginning, we believed that that was part of the media propaganda. However, between the 20th and 25th of August, we were certain that the scale of all this was considerable and that we had to do -- we had to take the most radical measures in order to prevent various criminal acts that were being committed in the liberated territory, including looting, the burning of houses, and individual murders committed by various criminal groups and individuals. We discussed this in the government, and we criticised it very strongly. I can say that after discussions with Minister Kinkel and many friends from the international community but also with the Helsinki committee of Croatia and representatives of the media and foreign ambassadors, including Mr. Peter Galbraith, that I personally also held talks with Mr. Jarnjak, who was the interior minister and who told me what the scope of these incidents was, and told me that, firstly, he needed more policemen, between 1500 to 3.000, but at least 1500, and that it was possible that -- that it was necessary to remove the military as soon as possible from the area. He said that the professional army was not committing any crimes or criminal acts and that it was necessary to carry out demobilisation as soon as possible and that there should be joint military and police patrols. I also discussed this with the prime minister, who supported the prevention of all this. I also had a long conversation with President Tudjman who told me that almost 200.000 soldiers were on the move, that it was very difficult to control the situation completely, but he personally promised me that he would do anything he could to stop these criminal acts and that he would issue an approval to Mr. Jarnjak for more policemen, that he would speed up the demobilisation of the military part of the army was already going to Bosnia-Herzegovina on the basis of the Split Declaration, and I also talked with Minister Susak who told me, Mate, these are not professional soldiers who are doing this. Shortly I also personally talked to the media representatives, and I urged them to report on this so that as soon as possible any crimes on the Croatian side and any criminal acts might be stopped. So this can be seen from the government sessions that were held at the time what our positions were. My personal position was that each one of us had to do anything that he or she could so that any criminal acts would be stopped as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The State of Croatia, faced with the fact of crimes which were being committed after the completion of the operation, reacted certainly through diplomatic channels as well, and now you will see that under tab 18 in your binder, Mr. Granic. utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could see the second part of this speech given by Mr. Simonovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph, we can see that he said that after a successful military operations, human rights were violated and the number of violations of human rights which were committed in the liberated areas of the Republic of Croatia against the remaining Serbian population, and that through legal processes initiated against these criminal acts and their perpetrators, the Croatian government has shown that the use of force was not the purpose, was not intended as retaliation, and to merely change the victims of human rights violations, but to ensure an efficient human rights protection for everyone through negotiations which began at the time; prosecution against over a thousand people for the alleged crimes was launched; and in order to restore confidence, the president of the Republic of Croatia pardoned 455 Croatian Serbs who participated in the armed rebellion against Croatia. Mr. Simonovic's speech in Geneva represents what sort of position? Was that his personal position, or does it articulate your positions and the positions of the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here articulated my positions and the positions of the government of the Republic of Croatia. It is undoubted that we were critical of everything that had taken place after the Operation Storm. And we were also taking steps, all steps that we could, in order to restore trust as soon as possible. I should note that this was taking place together with peaceful reintegration in the Danube basin in Croatia. And firstly we should see that the president pardoned more than 400 people, which resulted with a general amnesty and abolition for participation in armed rebellion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we have a look at the penultimate paragraph on this page, Mr. Simonovic says there that the Croatian government will facilitate the return of those Serbs who fled during military operations and who would now like to return. Mr. Granic, does this articulate the attitude of the government policy to all ethnic minorities in the Republic of Croatia including, of course, the Serbian ethnic minority?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's absolutely correct. This is a process that began, as we can see, very early on and which resulted in the Serbian community in Croatia having the highest level of legal protection. For six years it has been taking active part in the Croatian government. So from the very beginning it was a process that we believed in.

utterances.text: Yes. It was just the number that the then Minister Jarnjak mentioned was being prepared, three and a half thousand police officers. utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC

utterances.text: "In keeping with the state policy..." where exactly do we find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will try to find it, Your Honour. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's on the screen. It's the fourth line down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. It starts with "In keeping with the state policies..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've found it. Thank you. Yes. I see now that the language is as you read it, and I think it was, you said, criss-cross where it says this in English, but I found it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Next I would kindly ask the Registrar to move to page 4 of the English where we have Mr. Granic taking the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the Croatian, that is -- Dr. Granic says -- or, rather, you say, Mr. Granic, that: "The political decision was to launch a military and police action, and that was brought after the failure of the four-year negotiations with the Croatian Serbs in the occupied areas after the failure of both the UNPROFOR and UNCRO in the exercise of their mandates and in order to help Bihac which had been vitally endangered." This is already what we heard during your testimony about what you thought about it and what you said at that government session. That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I, nevertheless, come back to what you quoted. There are considerable differences between the language we find in the official translation. It's something "those who have been led astray for a period of four years," I do not -- I don't know what causes it. I have not looked at any original, but what you read is not by one or two words but is really not the same as what we see in the English translation of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, you are referring to the text which begins with "The political decision to launch a military and police action..." You're referring to that part of text?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I was told to -- that I would find the part you quoted on line 4 from the top. "In keeping with the state policies..." That's how it started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That was the previous one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the previous one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now I was citing speech of Dr. Granic which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but I'm still -- let me just -- I'm referring to page 42, starting on line 4. There you apparently quote what Mr. Susak had said, and you read: "In keeping with the state policy, the plan of action was to criss-cross the territory, avoiding residential areas, in the hope that those citizens of Croatia would surrender." Now, if I look at the document, it reads: "In keeping with the state policies, the operation was supposed to dissect the territory without touching populated settlements, hoping that the Croatian citizens who had been led astray during these four years..." Now, the last ten words do not appear in the quote you gave us. Now, it could be a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's the case, then at least quite a number of words were not translated to us. If that's the issue, then we leave it as it is. It has now been corrected. And you might consider this an encouragement to slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Granic, in the rest of your discussion, you -- you mentioned some media pressure whereby you say that it was stated that the columns were fired upon and the whole thing was a large ethnic cleansing operation with the figures being manipulated with and that there were more and more of those congratulating and saying that this operation was supposed to help resolve the problem in Bosnia as well.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. At that time, there was some media pressure, and there was a mention of the words ethnic cleansing, irrespective of the fact that the Serb population left voluntarily in a way that was planned and instigated by their leadership. And I have in mind specifically the time up to the 7th of August, 1995. There were no serious objections to our operation up to that time, save for the complaint that there -- that fire was opened on a column. That was rejected on our part. As for any political assessment, most expressed their satisfaction with the results of the operation. Why was that? Because it opened up new avenues to resolve the issue of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the creation of a lasting peace. And of course, needless to say, Bihac was saved as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After this, Dr. Granic, also on page 5 in the English text, you say in the discussion that President Tudjman invited our citizens of Serbian ethnicity to stay from the first moment and accepted also the law on amnesty, abolition, to surrender their weapons, and after that the government followed suit. And you conclude: "Therefore, we did everything to have the Serbian population remain in their homes, and we shall also invite all those who have not violated the norms of the International Law of War, that is to say those who have not committed war crimes, to return." Mr. Granic, this was the session held on the 7th of August. Did this interpretation continue later on after the completion of the Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was still the time when the Operation Storm was in progress, and it was our absolute strategic interest that the Serbian population who wished to stay and who had not committed any war crimes, that they should stay after the completion of the Operation Storm, and of course after the liberation of these areas, after the departure of one part of the Serbian population either to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is to say Republika Srpska. It was quite clear that with our citizens of Serbian ethnicity who were refugees that we could treat them in accordance with the international law and the international conventions and the experiences of the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask, Mr. President, that a number be assigned to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1813.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Would you allow me one clarifying question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want -- we've since found out that the previous document is not D1634. It actually is a different document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that still needs a number. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So I can be fully transparent on it, D1634, at page 5, contains, as a subset of it, the 3D document. So, hence, that's where the confusion comes from. I don't know how the Chamber wishes to proceed, because the pagination is now different in terms of how it was referred to with the witness, but I'll leave it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it would be better to assign a new number, because otherwise we -- there's a fair chance of confusion. Mr. Registrar, the previous document which, if you could please repeat the 3D number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was 3D00964, and it becomes Exhibit D1814.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1814 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Granic, on question: This meeting, 7th of August, bottom line being "We wanted the Serbs to stay," isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. At that moment, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this Chamber received evidence, I'm not going to evaluate all of that, but that some people say that all the Serbs that left had already left at that time, or at least if not for the full 100 per cent but that at least a great majority of the Serbs that did leave had left already on the 7th of August or were on their way to leave. Now, how do I have to understand the message "You Serbs stay" if they have departed already, if that would be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The majority had left, Your Honour. That is correct. However, as some of them were slowed down in the northern part of the territory, it made sense to send out a message to some of them who had not left yet. But it is true that the majority had left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're talking about the northern part of the territory, which territory are you referring to exactly? Would that include Sector South, northern parts of Sector South, or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Primarily it was the so-called Sector North. That was the UNPA area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because in this area the operations were slowed down, one entire corps had surrendered, and that was the reason why we were sending out such message, because there was still a chance that a part of the Serbian population would stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you especially had on your mind at that time those in that areas that had not yet left the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] I would ask the Registrar to show the document 3D00961.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Granic, that's tab 30 in your binder. We will see that these are the minutes from the 261st government session held on the 23rd of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if we could move on to page 10 of the English version and page 5 of the Croatian text where the words of Dr. Jure Radic are recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So Dr. Jure Radic, who talks here, as we can see on the previous page, says in the second paragraph of the text in English: "Secondly, both the president of the state and the prime minister and all of us together pointed out and called upon the Serbian population, citizens of the Croatian state, to stay in their areas. But it is worthwhile pointing out that many of them were expelled by the same aggressors who also expelled Croats from these liberated areas." Further, Dr. Radic talks about the majority of Croatian houses being destroyed, particularly in Kijevo, Lovinac, Skabrnja, Polaca, and Sveti Rok. And he says that -- he says Croatian houses, conditionally, houses which belong to the Croats in these areas, and further he says: "I would like here and now on behalf of the headquarters staff, and I'm certain the entire government shares my opinion, to distance myself from those individual cases of destruction of property, of Croatian property, even though it belonged to Serbs." And which has been taking place over the last few days, maybe the last week. Maybe not on a large scale but a scale which is visible, and I would ask the government to adopt very precise decisions about this that the Ministry of the Interior and Ministry of Defence would be in charge of so that that kind of destruction would be prevented and the perpetrators of these, as I call them, crimes be punished. Mr. Granic, that was the 23rd of August, so the government was obviously informed about unlawful acts being committed. And this was discussed at a government session. This was the proposal of Dr. Jure Radic that the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Defence should become more involved in the prevention of these crimes. According to your recollection of this period, what did the government do along these lines in the political sense and also at the diplomatic level?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a time when I would say during that particular week we received the first serious information from the ground that there were numerous incidents of criminal acts - and Jure Radic rightly called them crimes - that they were being committed on the Croatian side as well. And that this caused much damage to the Croatian government and the credibility of Croatia as a whole, and on the other hand, the proportions of the damage were great. The Ministry of the Interior was then charged to do everything that was necessary to stop this negative tendency, that is to say they were ordered by the government and the president of the republic to do everything they could to stop this development. That meant that they were entitled to increase the number of regular police officers in the area and that, in addition to that, the demobilisation was being stepped up at the time. I think that during two months the number of soldiers was reduced from 190.000 to 50.000. So that was a stepped-up demobilisation. Of course there were professional soldiers who were being sent to Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time in accordance with the Split Declaration, and these were also the strategic goals of the American peace initiative. And, of course, at the time, we also launched the media campaign, that this be reported about and that nothing should be covered up or hushed up -- none of the things that were happening on the ground. An additional factor at the time was that all the monitors who wished to go into this area were allowed to do so. We never prevented anyone from doing that because, regardless of how painful and difficult all of this was for us, we wished everyone from the international community to be able to go into the ground. Even though there were tendentious reports and there were exaggerations, it was a fact that this is what we requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, would you please take care that if you continue a quote which does not appear any more on our screen, that we move to the next page, because I now checked that what you read was a quote. It doesn't appear as a quote on the transcript itself. And, also, I noticed that what we seen in the original language apparently has got nothing to do with what is in the English language. I see numbering 1 to 8. So, therefore, for those who are following the proceedings in B/C/S, they would be confused as well. Could we take care that we always, on the screen, are focused on what you're asking the witness and what you're putting to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will do so, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Could we please move to page 21 of the English version, and that is page 32 of the Croatian version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What we can see on the top of the screen are the words of Mr. Bosiljko Misetic, which you can see several pages earlier. Mr. Misetic had what position in the government at the time?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the deputy prime minister in charge of the interior. The internal policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then he says -- it is at the top of the page both in the Croatian and English version. "The Croatian state showed its goodwill as far as these citizens are concerned, that they be citizens of Croatia which means and presupposes that it will protect every civil and human right of each citizens of the Croatian state with instruments of state authority and with other instruments in keeping with the provisions of the law, the constitutional law on the rights of the ethnic groups. And here some division or somewhere before, or somewhere before, the abolishing in places of whomever for his will to act. Every citizen of the State of Croatia had and still has the opportunity to become a Croatian citizen. Being a citizen means certain rights and certain obligations. The minimum they are asked to do is to accept the State of Croatia. "Every Serb who left had the opportunity. And the Croatian state is still giving them the opportunity to become citizens of the Croatian state. Those who do not want this will not do so of their own choice. It will be their own political will." Mr. Granic, for someone to be a citizen of the Republic of Croatia he has to possess certain documents; right?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what were the measures that the State of Croatia took so that the population of the liberated territories who had remained in these areas be issued personal documents? And we could see from the evidence that these were mostly elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For those who had remained there and who were elderly, regardless of the fact that we had some problems, because the land registers and the registers of births from many towns and municipalities had simply been taken away when the Serbian population departed during the Operation Storm, they could immediately be granted Croatian citizenship. And there was also another humanitarian operation to assist these people who had stayed there. That was a separate operation that was conducted. And when I say "assistance," that was how to provide them with medical, social, health care, how they could be issued documents. It was an organised and planned activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender this document into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1815.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. May I seek clarification of part of your quote. "Every citizen of the State of Croatia had and still has the opportunity to become a Croatian citizen." That's the quote, and I would like to ask you, Mr. Granic, what that line means. That if you're a Croatian citizen you have an opportunity to become a Croatian citizen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, simply, every citizen of Serbian ethnicity who was living in the occupied territories had the right to become a Croatian citizen. They did not use this right. Practically they had the citizenship of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. But considering where they had been born, that is to say in Croatia, they had a right to become Croatian citizens. And later on, all of them who wished so really were granted Croatian citizenship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So "every citizen" means every born inhabitant of Serbian origin being born in Croatia, living in Croatia, has an opportunity to become a Croatian citizen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I earlier asked you about the family reunion --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I earlier asked you about the return where no family member had left, how to reconcile that. First some plans had to be finalised, and you said it took two and a half years. You said this was a short period of time. And this language which suggests that if you're born here, just apply for citizenship and you're back -- you're back in town. How should I understand your previous answer in relation to this matter?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is all correct. Those Serbs who remained in the Republic of Croatia could be awarded citizenship immediately, and assistance was offered in particular to the elderly to have them enjoy that right as soon as possible. Those Croatian Serbs who left the occupied territories, becoming refugees, and who were also citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, for them this entailed a process in the plan of refugee return. We had to work on that in particular. There was one process of being issued with documents and another one having to do with the issue of return. We enclosed all that within that plan of refugee return. That was done together with the international community as well as the UNHCR and the ICRC. In the meantime, during the period when only the humanitarian issues of family reunion were being resolved, we also had individual return cases. There were quite many of them, although I don't know the exact figures. Someone specialised in that could be of more use. And I do know, however, that most of such requests were granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So to become a Croatian citizen, for those who had remained in the Krajina area, that was quickly to be done; but those who had left --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- there were two issues. First, getting the right papers to gain or perhaps regain -- most likely gain Croatian citizenship, and then that did not automatically mean that they then could immediately return, because the mass return, as you said, had to be prepared by agreements first and that took approximately two and a half years. Although, in individual cases, some people could return.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. Most of the individual cases were dealt with that way. If they provided any guarantee that they would be received by other family members in Croatia, such cases were automatically granted. In addition to that, the international community took part as well. This was an ongoing return process. However, the impetus was created only once the plan and programme for return was -- once it was put in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That refers to one of your previous answers you've given. Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let's stay with this topic a bit longer, Mr. Granic, although you're not a specialist in administrative matters, although, you may be able to answer some of my questions, and this in relation to the President's questions. After Croatia became an independent state in 1991, is it correct that all Croatian citizens, irrespective of their ethnicity, were supposed to ask for new documents in keeping with the fact that this was a new state?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That applies to everyone. No distinction was made from the very beginning. Quite the contrary. We would have been quite happy had the Serbs in occupied territories asked for the new documents. So we would have been very happy to grant them that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But the Serbs who lived in the territory of the so-called Republika Srpska Krajina physically could not ask to be issued with Croatian identity papers because they had no point of contact with the Croatian authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Simply put, the Serbs in the occupied territories and their representatives were ready, during the talks, to discuss different economic issues under the pressure of the international community, I believe; but they were never ready to discuss political matters such as the issue of reintegration and bringing the territory within the framework of the Republic of Croatia. Although, there were such individual instances of people approving of that but never en masse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Another thing, you've already mentioned it before, but perhaps it wouldn't hurt to go back to it. There was an important problem in that all registry books with citizen data in the newly liberated area of the former Serbian Krajina were either taken away or destroyed. There were grave problems with the identification of persons; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the books were taken away. As far as I know, it wasn't always the case, but for the most part it was so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it's about the third leading question in a row.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I would say for today, in counting, I'm far above three, as a matter of fact, Mr. Waespi, but you did not object to many of them. Mr. Mikulicic, I noted that -- and, of course, I asked myself why there were no objections often raised by Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Because it's obvious, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or if it is obvious and if Mr. Waespi doesn't disagree, it might be that these are mainly matters which are not that much in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I don't know in advance whether Mr. Waespi will disagree or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think it's for the first day that we're hearing evidence in this case. So what is in dispute and what is not in dispute on these matters may be clearer than you suggest at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can assure you my only intention was to speed up the proceedings, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So I'm apologising, of course, to Mr. Waespi, and I'll try to avoid any leading questions in the future, especially when I'm just about to finish my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to seek clarification. When you said that it was physically impossible for persons of Serb ethnicity, once Croatia had become an independent state, to apply for Croatian papers, was the same true for citizens of Croatian origin?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but that was referring only to those Serbs who were living in the Krajina territory, so the occupied territory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I am --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- not for the other Serbs who were living on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear to me. I'm also referring to the Croatians who remained to live in the area of the -- as is often said, the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina. Did they have similar problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood your question perfectly well. That is correct. The same applied to both Croats and Serbs. We would have been happy for the Croats from that territory to ask for those documents, much as the Serbs, for them to be able to get out of the territory and ask for such documents. That would have been a sign to us indicating that the Serbs were looking to reach a solution on peaceful reintegration. There were such rare and individual situations but never en masse, because in the occupied territory there was the Martic government as well as that of his associates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So once the Republic of Croatia had regained power in the Sector South in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, the situation was that both persons of Serb ethnicity but also persons of Croat ethnicity were not registered as Croatian citizens at that time. So the Croats had to register again and apply for papers as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Correct. Those who did not do it earlier, although the number of remaining Croats was not great. This was practically an ethnically cleansed area. It is true, however, there were a number of them, but the same procedure applied to both Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Granic -- before that I would like to have this document admitted. No, it seems it was admitted already. No, it wasn't. So first I ask permission to include it on the 65 ter list, and then I would like to ask for an exhibit number. It is 3D00961.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It's already an exhibit, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're right, Mr. Mikulicic. And there's no need to ask again leave to add documents to the 65 ter list, because I think at the beginning of today I said that all the documents not on the 65 ter list, that leave is granted in advance in view of the absence of any objections by Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, I'm nearing the end of my examination. I'd like to ask you now to answer the following question: Having been present at government meeting and various other meetings, be it with the president of the republic, be it the meeting of the National Council -- National Security Council, was there ever raised the issue of Special Police at these meetings and any sort of misconduct on the part of the Special Police Units?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had not heard that. The Special Police Units were highly esteemed. Since I was the prime minister [as interpreted] since the 3rd of August, 1991, I knew that the Special Police Units had been involved in very difficult missions as an elite unit. And even later on it was reputed to be a highly disciplined force which carried out some of the most difficult tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you personally know General Markac at the time?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew him as of 1991 as an honourable individual of moral integrity who headed the Special Police force and was highly esteemed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to talk to him personally?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your conversations with General Markac, did you ever notice or observe on his part any sort of animosity or prejudice toward Croatian citizens of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard anything of the sort. Had I heard something like that, I would have reacted right away, but I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers, Mr. Granic. I've finished my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for the transcript, I don't think it's in dispute, but page 61, line 16, the witness was deputy prime minister, and I believe that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There seems to be no confusion about that. Then next in line. Mr. Misetic, it will be you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Granic. I should say good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, I'm going to take you through the events, focusing mostly on August 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But first let me call up Exhibit P462, please. Actually, I'm sorry, P456. I apologise, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a meeting, Mr. Granic, where you were present. It's dated 11 August. And present with you are President Tudjman, Minister Susak, Minister Jarnjak. And as someone who participated in the meeting, I'd just like you to read one section of the document and tell us what your interpretation of it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this is at page 6 in the Croatian and page 3 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd ask you if you could review Minister Jarnjak's comment there at the paragraph that you see now on your screen that starts "From Zagreb, Pupovac was making a fuss..." if you could read that. It says: "Pupovac called around saying it's a catastrophe there. They're killing them with clubs, beating them, pounding. He got a call from a woman who said that 99 per cent of all Serbs who went through Sisak were beaten. That's horrible and we need to do something about that. They called everybody. Djukic called me yesterday. I wasn't there. He probably wanted to say something about that too. And Dzakula, that son of a bitch, is right on Pupovac's line and he does everything that Pupovac tells him." Can you explain, Mr. Granic, the context there and why is Mr. Jarnjak -- or what was your understanding of why Mr. Jarnjak was upset with Mr. Pupovac and Mr. Dzakula?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jarnjak was the minister of the interior, and he believed that representatives of the Serb community at that time, on the 11th of August, were snowballing the problems. They were exaggerating them at that point in time with regard to the departure of the Serb population and the alleged attacks on them. The minister wanted to say that they took the issue out of all proportion, and that's the all -- the only way that I can understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you have any understanding that Minister Jarnjak was upset with them because they were being truthful in their allegations?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. There certainly were incidents, especially on the way through Sisak. There quite certainly were, however, none of the incidents resulted in death. At any rate, we took note of it. And one of the pieces of information that Jarnjak took into account and everyone when deciding what needed to be done next in order to make sure that on the one hand these incidents do not happen again and that on the other the international community be informed properly. Of course, we were under enormous pressure from the international community, because the general belief was that ethnic cleansing was being carried out, which was not the truth. It is certainly true that the Serb population was leaving because they were encouraged to do so. There were among them those who didn't accept the Croatian state and who had been absolutely indoctrinated for the previous ten years. At least until --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the year that you mentioned at the end of your answer, Mr. Granic?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1987. Ever since Milosevic came to power.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar if we could have on the screen, please, Exhibit D1635, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, this is a US code cable, and if you look at the fourth line from the top you'll see that there is a date there which is 6 August 1995 at 1530 hours is when it's sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says -- and, again, this is 6 August: "Croatian foreign minister Mate Granic told the ambassador that the government of Croatia and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina would co-operate militarily in Bosnia ..." And then towards the middle it says: "Granic said that the Bosnian-Croatian militia, HVO supported by the Croatian Army, would continue military campaigns towards Drvar, Donji Vakuf, and Jajce. They would move -- then move to push Serb artillery away from Mostar and Dubrovnik. Afterwards, they will, in consultation with the international community, mainly the United States, help to open the Sarajevo corridor." Now, if we could turn to Exhibit D296, please. This is a presidential transcript from the 7th of August, which would be the next day after that US code cable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn, sorry, to page 15 in the English and page 31 in the Croatian, please. Sorry. If we could go to page 14 in the English, please. I believe it should be the previous page in the B/C/S then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Granic, if you look at the middle of the page in the English - we're having trouble finding it in the B/C/S, in the Croatian - but it says, you report that: "The US will be extremely interested now, and that is of why it is of vital importance that you hold your talks with Izetbegovic as soon as possible to strategically handle the overall situation. And now every day from tomorrow on, every day will be precious as far as that is concerned. I think we have to reach, as soon as possible, a final strategic ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then if we could turn to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There is a discussion then that continues about consultations with the Bosnian government. And then at the bottom Dr. Zuzul says in that paragraph at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Page 31 in the Croatian please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zuzul says: "Yesterday, I explicitly asked what was going on in the southern part. There's no problem with the HVO going down there, but, if possible, not the Croatian Army." And he's referring here to his consultation was the United States government. "And their discussion was to --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Their discussion was to do Donji Vakuf and Jajce together with the Muslims." Now, Donji Vakuf and Jajce are towns in Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And it continues on: "They even suggest that, just make sure that our army don't cross now that we've liberated this area towards Bihac, make sure they don't cross over ... I didn't ask about Drvar, but this was because this story about how Bosnia and Herzegovina will now actually be divided with the help of the Americans is looming large and how they let us do that." Now, Minister Granic, today at transcript page 46, lines 13 to 16, you said that: "Operation Storm opened up new avenues to resolve the issue of war in Bosnia and the creation of lasting peace." Now, I'd like to ask you -- having reviewed what your comments were to Ambassador Galbraith on the 6th and this discussion on the 7th internally at the top of the Croatian leadership about moving into Bosnia and operating then to take towns in Western Bosnia, elaborate further. Explain more specifically what was it about Operation Storm that created the conditions to resolve the issue of war in Bosnia and -- that's the first question. The second question is: What was the strategic aim of the government of Croatia in immediately planning on operations in Bosnia before Operation Storm had even finished?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I have seen here is correct. Our first strategic goal was to help lift the blockade of Bihac. The other strategic goals were to help the Croats and Bosniaks liberate the occupied areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was the goal of the American peace initiative, too, because without it Milosevic would never have agreed to negotiate. And this was especially true for Karadzic. He would never have agreed to negotiate without it. Every day we were in contact with the highest ranking officials of the United States on the diplomatic level, which was done by myself and the then Ambassador Zuzul. On the ministry level, that was Mr. Susak with William Perry, the Defence Secretary at the intelligence level and many other levels. Therefore, not a step was taken after without these consultations.
