And the consultations had to do with which town should be headed toward by the BH army rather than the Croat army in terms of Vakuf and so on and so forth. But, at any rate, strategic agreements were made about how far one could go. Let me raise one issue which I believe will be helpful to the Trial Chamber. When the Croatian Army, the BH Army, and the HVO reached Banja Luka, the State secretary Christopher, and I think it was around the 14th of October, 1995, I think it was round about that time, called me, and Mr. Holbrooke called President Tudjman. He told me, "Mate, please stop there." I told him that I was not the supreme commander and that I could merely convey my opinion to President Tudjman as the supreme commander. The state secretary told me in reply that if we should not stop, and we only needed two days to liberate Banja Luka and Posavina, as he put it, a humanitarian catastrophe would ensue. 350.000 persons would leave. Almost 100.000 of them would go to Eastern Slavonija and Baranja as well. Milosevic would be destabilised as a partner, and the Dayton Accords were already being prepared. After that, the state secretary Christopher and Holbrooke called the president who accepted their suggestion. This was only one of the indications and absolute evidence that we fully co-operated with the international community and with the US in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, let me ask you, from the Split agreement in late July, until the operation stopped on the outskirts of Banja Luka as you've now mentioned, was it understood what General Gotovina's role would be in implementing these strategic objectives in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I was the minister of foreign affairs and this was not my duty, but, diplomatically speaking, Bosnia-Herzegovina was my primary task, hence I am quite familiar with these issues as well. General Gotovina was reputed to be an excellent general, a disciplined general who was suitable for the most difficult of missions. So I wasn't -- it didn't come as a surprise to me at all when the president said that the southern axis, the most important, would be would be headed by General Gotovina as would be the operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was something that I expected, and I found perfectly normal. These were the most significant operations to be carried out by the Croatian Army. So it doesn't come as a surprise to me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that what you were agreeing with the United States and discussing with the United States at a strategic level was actually being implemented on the ground by General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's completely true. As you can see from the American sources, what I said on the 6th, and I think that that was precisely what this particular source referred to, it was a strategic objective which enjoyed full support of the United States of America. Had it been otherwise, I would have received a caution right away. We didn't -- we didn't make a single move without co-operation with the USA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know when we're going to address the matter that the Cermak Defence wishes to raise, whether it's now or at the beginning of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could do it now. Mr. Granic, we have to deal with a procedural matter. I, therefore, will ask that you be escorted out of the courtroom. It also means that your break will be a bit longer than ours, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, is it you who will raise the issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The issue that I wish to raise briefly concerns the Martic schedule of agreed facts which Your Honour is already aware of. A dispute arose two days ago, and it's perhaps worth setting out a brief chronology so that the Bench is aware of the efforts that have been made by the Defence in this regard. Your Honour will be aware that on the 2nd of October, 2009, the Cermak Defence team filed seven motions which ran to a total of 1.374 pages, six of which were under Rule 92 bis and one of which was under Rule 92 quater. Under Your Honours' guidance, on the 9th of October, 2009, transcript page 22866 to 22869, the Defence and the Prosecution were invited to explore other avenues for admission of that evidence. And the Chamber indicated that it considered that the most appropriate way for the Cermak Defence to present the relevant and important portions was through the route of agreed facts. Now, subsequent to the guidance that we received, we sent the Prosecution the first version of the schedule of evidence on the 16th of October of this year. The Prosecution responded on the 22nd of October, suggesting that we perhaps only rely on what we could have supported from the Martic judgement as opposed to citing witness evidence and testimony and transcript. We took that suggestion on board, and we spent several days reworking the entire schedule itself so that it would reflect the Martic judgement references. Our revised schedule was then sent to the Prosecution on the 26th of October. And on the 28th of October, Prosecution suggested that we add a map so that it was clear to everyone where these locations could be found for ease of reference. A final version of the evidence schedule was agreed and cleared of any typographical errors on the 10th of November, and that was agreed between ourselves and Mr. Waespi on behalf of the Prosecution. So far so good. However, from that stage, we then tried to put a brief motion together that could accompany the table in which we proposed that the table itself should, of course, be admitted into evidence and form part of the trial record and given an exhibit number. That brief proposed motion was sent to the Prosecution on the 11th of November, and it's our recollection that we didn't get any response to that until the deadline set by Your Honour, which was the 16th of November, several days ago. Unfortunately, it seems that this marked the start of the dissent in which it was the first time raised by the Prosecution that Appendix A, which is the schedule of agreed facts, should not be admitted into evidence but simply that the Bench should take note of the facts. Our position is very much that the schedule that came from evidence constitutes evidence as agreed facts and should be admitted by the Trial Chamber as well as the map over which there is no dispute. The map, however, simply being geographically reflective of the contents of the agreed facts. As we understand it, as I've said, the position of the Prosecution is that the schedule itself should not be admitted. We pray in aid, in support of our approach, two decisions, one of which is the Perisic decision, dated the 30th of September, 2009, in which the Chamber there admitted the agreed facts under Rule 65 ter (H), 65 ter (M), and Rule 89(C) as it deemed that the agreed facts were relevant and probative to the case. And it, therefore, admitted the facts as part of the record. The second case which we pray in aid is the Blagojevic decision of the 19th of December, 2003. Again it concerned, in fact, issues of judicial notice and agreed facts. At paragraph 13 of that decision, the Trial Chamber found that the recording of points of agreement during the trial phase results in the acceptance of those agreed points as evidence under Rule 89(C). Now, in the event that we have not been able to, ourselves, determine how the Chamber should deal with this issue, I have set out our proposal. And we can, of course, provide the Bench with copies of the decisions upon which we rely. And we would ask the Bench to simply admit both schedules, the agreed facts and the map. Mr. Waespi was on notice of this point yesterday as it was, unfortunately, a rally of e-mails between ourselves during the course of which it became clear that our approaches differed. And I'm sorry that this matter has had to come before the Bench, as it should have been something that we should have been able to work out. I hope our submissions are clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are. But if they still are after we've heard Mr. Waespi, still remains to be seen. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I agree with my colleague that a lot of effort went into these project but not just on the Defence side, also from the Prosecution side. We created a map. A lot of errors had to be corrected just to make that clear. The Prosecution would like to emphasise up front that we have no ill-intent in regard to the debate over how to treat agreed facts. The only intention from our side it to ensure that the record is clear and to preserve the integrity of the evidentiary process. In our submission, the parties' agreed facts are not evidence. On the contrary, the purpose of the agreement between the parties is to obviate the need for evidence on points that are not in dispute. Since the agreed facts do not constitute evidence, it would be improper to tender this document, the agreed facts, not the map, into evidence and to give it an exhibit number. Instead, this document should be filed. Filing the document does not change its status as part of the trial record. The Defence may still refer to the agreed facts in setting forth its legal arguments in the final brief or closing statements. Even though the agreed facts are not marked as an exhibit, the Defence should be assured that the Prosecution will not dispute the facts or seek to introduce evidence contrary to the facts. Indeed, the Trial Chamber would surely reprimand the Prosecution if it made any attempt to undermine these agreed facts. The procedural difference between filing the agreed facts and tendering it as evidence does not change the undisputed nature of the facts, nor does it undercut the extent to which the Defence may rely on these facts. Your Honours, I've looked randomly yesterday at the few trial judgements, how they deal with agreed facts or stipulation in their footnotes, and I looked at the Blagojevic, the case my colleague cited. In footnote 650 of the Blagojevic trial judgement of 17 January 2005, we have a reference to agreed facts para 135. So it's not been exhibited. Similarly, in the Dragomir Milosevic case, footnote 17, also trial judgement. Galic case, footnote 344, as regards the stipulations. And the Krajisnik judgement, footnote 259, again trial admissions by the accused. The only case I found again that was really a random selection was the Oric case, Trial Chamber, footnote 146 ter. Agreed facts have received and are referred to as exhibits, although I only looked just at the footnote itself. I didn't look at the actual exhibit. The case my colleague mentioned, the Perisic case, the agreed facts were eventually not given exhibit numbers, as I understand it. It's correct that the decision itself refers to having it exhibited, but apparently it has not received an exhibit number. That's what our inquiry resulted. Obviously the Perisic case is still ongoing. These are my submissions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to understand what keeps you apart. You, Ms. Higgins, you say these -- this document in which we have described jointly what we agree upon should be admitted into evidence. And you, Mr. Waespi, you say, We still agree on these facts, but they should not be evidence. Let me first then go back to what apparently evidence is. Isn't it true that evidence information in whatever form, either contained in documents or in oral testimony or on video, whatever, material information in that specific format as presented which can be considered by the Chamber if it deliberates on factual findings? Would everyone agree on this to be the basic notion of what evidence is? Second step is admission into evidence, I would say primarily gains its -- gets its meaning in allowing this information in that specific format to come to be accessible to the trier of facts and the admission of evidence primarily is matter which plays a role in adversarial and I would even say jury trials. That is the decision. This is information, material, video, whatever, which is available to the jury in its -- for its fact-finding purposes. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now let's go to agreed facts. Isn't the basis for the agreed facts that the parties say that, "We consider that the Chamber can establish the facts we agreed upon without any evidence, that is, information supporting the finding of those facts. We parties, having looked at either evidence which was presented, or having considered material which has not been presented as evidence to the Court, on the basis of that, we both agree that a Chamber could make a factual finding of the following sort." And then you set out the agreed facts. Therefore, an agreement on facts may find its basis in material which is admitted into evidence but also may find its basis in material which is not in evidence or even exclusively on material which is not in evidence. Then finally, it is for the Chamber to see whether it adopts, either on the basis of the agreement of the parties or in the context of evidence, to adopt or not to adopt a factual finding, as the parties suggest the Chamber could, perhaps even should, adopt. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that it is evidence that the Bench must then take as evidence and draw its own conclusions therefrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now the only thing that keeps you apart is whether you call that evidence or not. In my analysis, I said that the Bench would have to consider, on the basis of the totality of the evidence or on whatever basis, whether these facts, which it could adopt without hearing any further evidence on it, whether it adopts it, yes or no. It's finally for the Chamber to decide. Now, it seems that you give a different meaning to what the latitude would be of the Chamber to -- to consider that material or not to consider that material, and that apparently seems to be your concern, Ms. Higgins. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. My concerning lies, if I may just elaborate a little, on the fact that my learned friend speaks of transparency of the proceedings. And for us to understand the transparency of the proceedings, the best way to proceed, we say, is to follow prior examples of where the agreed facts have been stated to be evidence which has been admitted under Rule 65 ter (H) and (M) and Rule 89(C). We say it's clear evidence. And, therefore, whether Your Honour admits the schedule or has the document as a filing, we are just concerned that it is given the label of "evidence," particularly given that it came from an abundance of evidence which we were seeking to initially put before this Chamber. We feel that we have been restricted down to the bear minimum. And then to have the other party say that this is not going to be admitted onto the record seems to be disingenuous and seems to have restricted our hand in the way we best present our evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, earlier I tried to understand what it means that something is admitted into evidence. That is that it comes to the jury. Now, isn't it a semantic issue that whether the matter comes to this Trial Chamber upon an invitation to agree on these facts where it's clear to both parties that exclusively on the basis of that agreement the Chamber can, the parties may even think should, adopt those facts as facts it found, even if there's no further basis for that? At the say time, the Chamber - and I think the parties agree on that as well - is not bound by the agreement of the parties if, for any good reason - I'm not saying for any reason but for any good reason - we would choose not to adopt such facts, we're free to do so, just as we would be on the basis of the evidence underlying, whether known to us or unknown to us, to adopt similar conclusions as the parties apparently have done. We're free to finally decide what to do and what not to do. But the way in which it is presented, whether as evidence or whether as a filing of agreed facts, I cannot - but I will discuss the matter with my colleagues - I cannot see yet what difference it would make. That would mean that accepting it as evidence is a bit odd in the context of the definition of "evidence" I just gave, that is, evidence is information which is used to establish facts. We're already beyond that, because a logic -- the evidence, known or unknown to the Chamber, already led the parties to draw conclusions that this is sufficient to establish or to find facts A, B, or C. Now, therefore, I see that -- I see your concerns, and these concerns, I think, depend on the way in which the Chamber would look at a difference. Up until this moment, I do not see that we would approach either through the one technique - I call it technique - or the other technique, that we would make any difference. But I will discuss this with my colleagues. Any further submissions in this respect? First --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Just in relation to the deadline, that was, I think, today, we need directions on how to -- to sign it, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may know my approach to these matters, that if there is a matter which I'd consider the parties could settle but are unable to settle, I always offer my good services at meetings at 7.00 in the morning where we certainly will find a solution for them. That offer is a standing offer, is always there, but I saw that Mr. Kehoe was on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Given this position by the Office of the Prosecutor, it certainly has given me pause, because we have entered into any number of stipulations with the Office of the Prosecutor on any number of facts. And up until this morning or until the rally of e-mails back and forth that my learned friend Ms. Higgins alluded to just moments ago, we were of the belief that that was stipulated facts that were part of the evidentiary record which the Chamber could accept or reject as it decided. But never were we thinking that the stipulations or agreements on certain issues were somehow outside of the evidentiary arena, and frankly, Mr. President, given the position by the Prosecution, I don't know what category these stipulated facts or the facts that Ms. Higgins was discussing fall into if they are not evidence. So with regard to the Chamber ultimately make a decision, with the caveat, of course, that the Chamber can accept or reject any stipulated fact as it so chooses, it seems to me that this change of position is giving the Prosecution some way to opt out of the evidentiary arena as opposed to putting this in the evidentiary arena. So, while I appreciate, Your Honour, that the discussion may be some exercise in mental gymnastics, and you appreciate what Your Honour is saying in that regard, it gives me some pause as to where we are with regard to all of these other issues that we have been discussing since March of 2008, because this is clearly a different position articulated by the Prosecution. And frankly, Your Honour, I don't know what the answer is, I just want to raise those concerns and echo the concerns raised by my learned friend Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As I said before, I will consult with my colleagues. I'll try to see whether we agree, more or less, on the basis of evidence and factual findings. Mr. Kehoe, it is as with the flu: If we find a problem here, immediately all the rest is affected by it as well. So, therefore, we try to resolve it so that no one gets ill.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. Your Honour may be assisted by the Blagojevic decision, which I'm happy to provide copies to the Bench, because it deals with not only the methods by which evidence may come before the Court at paragraph 9, which includes the admission of facts under 65 ter (H), but it also defined in paragraph 12 what it means to admit facts, thereby removing those points from the spheres of judicial inquiry during trial. They are accepted into the proceedings, and the matter to which the agreed facts relates ceases to be a disputed issue. If that would assist the Chamber, I can, of course, hand up the two decisions I referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to save paper and since it is my preference to look at -- perhaps if you have one copy, that would assist. Now, my last observation is that, of course, Rule 65 ter (H), although quoted, doesn't say anything about whether that is evidence or is not evidence, it's just that points of agreement, and disagreement, by the way, on matters of law and fact shall be recorded by the Pre-Trial Judge. It doesn't say much more. And that the Chamber could order to -- order the parties to file written submissions on the matter. Now, I would say this is a rather typical lawyer situation. It seems that there's agreement on at least the substance, but we, of course, always find procedural ways to see whether there's any disagreement. The Chamber will consider the matter and will come back to the parties. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Because I'm a lawyer, I have to make clear that there was no change in position as advocated by Mr. Kehoe in relation to whether agreed facts shall be trial exhibits or not. Just to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The deadline is not the matter that is of greatest concern at this moment. The Chamber appreciates that at least the parties have agreed on a formulation of facts they agree upon. We will have a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed by Mr. Registrar that a courtroom is available tomorrow afternoon. Staffing is there as well. Whether the Judges are available is still to be seen. I certainly need for another matter at least half an hour, but then still there would be quite some time available. At the same time, I repeat what I said earlier to making these -- to engage in these exercises claiming more courtroom time, et cetera, et cetera. First of all, we'll only do it if the parties commit themselves to finishing the testimony of Mr. Granic this week. Of course, with all reservations that unforeseen -- unforeseen circumstances can never be excluded, but I then expect a firm commitment. The second is that I also would not appreciate if the parties would claim additional time in court and then to find out that, by the end of this week, that there actually had been no need to do all this. So we do it if it achieves a goal, and then we need the parties to commit to achieving that goal, and if that goal can be achieved without this additional exercise, we should do without. We have a break, and we resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to inform the parties, first of all, that we will give you the guidance needed, Ms. Higgins and Mr. Waespi, soon. Give us a bit more time. But from what we discussed until now, there will not remain any problem as far as the Chamber is concerned. Then the second issue is scheduling for this week. We checked the availability of tomorrow in the afternoon. First of all, if we would sit tomorrow in the afternoon, it would be under 15 bis because all of the Judges is not available. The Chamber prefers not to sit under Rule 15 bis, but we'll do so if that would contribute in achieving the aim of finishing the testimony of Mr. Granic. The Chamber also made an assessment. One the other Judges, by the way, is temporarily not available, which means that most likely we couldn't start any earlier than 3.30 or 3.45, and in assessing the times -- the time estimates given by the parties, the Chamber takes the view now that most likely two sessions tomorrow in the afternoon would more or less do the job, but again we'd rather do without and conclude the testimony anyhow, but our assessment is that at least with two session tomorrow afternoon we might be able to conclude the testimony this week. Finally, the Chamber invites the parties, Prosecution and Defence, to work out a further schedule in order to see whether it's really needed, as I said before, and also that there is a clear schedule, then, this party until that moment that party from 2.00 to 5.00, whatever, so that we have a clear schedule, that you agree upon it. If you can't reach any agreement, of course, the Chamber will finally settle the matter. But the parties are invited to deliver such a schedule by 3.00 this afternoon. So to work that out immediately after this session, because the Registry should know whether they should reserve time, whether they should have everyone ready to assist us. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There are just a lot of uncertainties also. I'm thinking about redirect. Obviously my cross-examination will be substantial, and so there is a potential for -- for some redirect. And it's -- I'm just wondering whether it wouldn't be an option that the witness could stay longer on Friday afternoon, that we are committed without tomorrow's session to finish by lunchtime tomorrow as planned, and if not go into -- into Friday afternoon if we really need that. And I don't know exactly what the witness's plans are also, you know, for Monday, but this is -- it's, as you know, an enormous strain on all participants to then work morning, afternoon, Friday without interruption. Of course we'll do it and I'm happy to talk with the Defence after court, but it's very difficult to assess and actually allocate what the parties -- the time the parties end. That's just my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, of course, we all have sufficient experience to calculate, even on a provisional basis, some time for re-examination. That -- we'll ask the witness, but, of course, the Chamber, apart from this witness, also has some concern to lose pace in the presentation of evidence. And I think three witnesses were schedule for this week. Then we lose already one. We then lose more time even in the beginning of next week. And the Chamber is really determined to move on as efficiently as possible, of course always within the context of the frame of the fair trial issue. The strain is felt not only by the parties but by the Chamber as well. Mr. Granic, you may have noticed that we discussed to some extent also some of your fate. The Chamber is trying hard to push the parties to see that we can conclude your evidence this week. If we would not achieve that, would it cause you major problems to stay over the weekend and to remain available on Monday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that would present a significant problem to me. If possible, I would prefer to have my testimony concluded by Friday afternoon so that on Friday afternoon I would be able to travel, if in any way possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's a strong preference. We share that preference with you, but it would not be totally impossible. You said this would cause you major problems, but major problems are not always insurmountable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I have to consult with Zagreb first in order to be able to give you an answer tomorrow. I would prefer, nevertheless, if possible, to have it concluded by Friday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear, Mr. Granic. Let's then try to move forward as quickly as possible. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit P453 on the screen please. And I'm particularly interested in page 2 in the English and page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, this is a transcript of a conversation with -- presidential transcript of 16 August between Mr. Holbrooke, Mr. Fraser, General Clark, Mr. Galbraith, President Tudjman, yourself, Minister Susak, and others. First I'm interested in -- let's see. Yes. There's a sentence in the original --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 4 in the Croatian. The bottom of page 2 in the English. Next page in the Croatian, please, and the bottom of page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, he's -- Mr. Holbrooke is discussing --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could we scroll to the top of the Croatian, please. There we go. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You see the word Czechoslovakia in the upper middle part of the page. Mr. Holbrooke is discussing the future of Bosnia, and he says: "However, whatever the outcome, we think that the present borders, the present international borders in that area should not be altered unless they are altered voluntarily as in the case of the 'divorce' of Czechoslovakia. That is all right. The manner in which Czechoslovakia parted is all right, but non-voluntary changes in the borders are a mistake and this is vitally important when we talk about Slavonia."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page in English please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I'll come back to this entry in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But if we could now go to page 7 in the Croatian and page 4 in the English, please. And this is at the very top in the Croatian. Sorry, page -- numbered page 7, so one more page forward in the Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And in the English it's the paragraph that begins "Fourthly." And in the Croatian it's the first full sentence at the top of the page. In the middle of the English page, Mr. President Holbrooke says: "We have read contradictory reports of abuses at the local level in connection with the departure of Serbs from the Krajina, reports of burning houses, mistreatment, et cetera. I know that many of these -- those reports are exaggerated. Journalists tend to exaggerate, but the accusations of ethnic cleansing in this regard harm our goal as regards constitutional arrangements." Now, in your testimony today, Mr. Granic, you have also made reference several times -- at transcript page 25, lines 18 to 19, you said that with respect to these reports of crimes, we believe this was propaganda. At transcript page 18, line 16, you stated that the British minister of defence's comments that were in contradiction to the British ambassador to Croatia's assessment, was because Portillo gave his comments on a strategic level, and I'd like to explore this issue a little bit. Mr. Holbrooke indicated to President Tudjman that he felt these reports were exaggerated, and he then connects it to how these reports are harming our goal as regards constitutional arrangements. You've indicated that Mr. Portillo may have had a strategic reason for claiming that Croatia was engaged in ethnic cleansing. Can you explain that a little bit more? Why are exaggerated reports or claims of ethnic cleansing -- why would they be in someone's strategic interest?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both of these reports indicate the same thing, and that is that during and immediately after Operation Storm, we had two things on our mind. Firstly, how to peacefully reintegrate Eastern Slavonija on the one hand; and on the other, how to assist Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to stop the war and establish peace there. Croatia was an important part of the American peace initiative. The American peace initiative went contrary to the previous efforts of the international community under the leadership of the co-chairpersons Owen and Stoltenberg. That plan, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan fell through. I have to say here that as early as 1994 in New York, Lord Owen told me once that it was impossible to achieve peace and reintegration of the occupied territory without territorial concessions by Croatia. This, in turn, meant to give an exit, open exit, to the sea to the Bosnians as well as to open up a corridor of at least 20 kilometres in which just below Zupanja and that parts of Eastern Slavonija either be part of Croatia or that a condominium arrangement be put in place. That was the reason why Ambassador Holbrooke clearly stated that he was against the change of borders. And Croatia stood firmly behind that. By the same token, the strategic goal in Bosnia and Herzegovina was to have a powerful functioning B and H federation when we negotiated in Washington. Our goal was to expand the model across the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina as a decentralised single state, and that state was supposed to encompass the whole Bosnia and Herzegovina and would be based on a federation model. There were differences between the UK and the US in terms of their strategic views of how the war should be stopped and peace achieved in Bosnia-Herzegovina. As for the model of the equation of guilt is something which went to the detriment of Croatian interests as well as its credibility. The credibility of Croatia was very important to the US in order to achieve the strategic goals in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the joint military operations of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the HVO, and the HV.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you explain further how -- I'm going to assume that -- I asked you specifically about Minister Portillo's comments, and you've indicated that the equalisation of guilt - and I assume by that you meant equalisation of guilt between the Serb side and the Croatian side - that this would harm the credibility of Croatia. Let's take it the next step. Why -- how does the discrediting of Croatia then affect or promote someone else's strategic aim? Let's take the concrete example of Minister Portillo. Can you explain what some people had to gain by discrediting the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, almost 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was controlled by Karadzic's Serbs. There was no chance for a peaceful settlement without the B and H federation, or, in other words, a federation of Bosniaks and Croats freeing at least part of that territory. That was crystal clear. By reducing the credibility of Croatia, this possibility of joint operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina was supposed to be diminished. And, in turn, the US support to those operations would be reduced accordingly. I must state yet again that concerning the Srebrenica crisis, there was no use of NATO military force in order to prevent it from happening. This was not allowed by either the generals or by Mr. Akashi. In turn it proved to be tragic. We know the results of the UN investigation which was an objective investigation. We are all familiar with its results. In other words, we were aware that we had to embark upon this operation alone if we wanted to help Bihac and liberate Croatia and if we wanted to assist the strategic intentions of the American peace initiative in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Granic. Since we've opened up this topic, let me jump, right now, to a document, that is, 65 ter 4606. And I'll be making references to this document both today and tomorrow. Mr. Granic, this is a presidential transcript recording a telephone conversation between President Tudjman and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on the 25th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 in the English, please. That's correct. And scroll to the bottom in the English and to the bottom in Croatian as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As you can see and read, they greet each other, and Chancellor Kohl says -- he says actually in the middle: "However, you have a lot of friends, I have three things that I would like to discuss with you today." The president says: "Yes, please? "The first one is something which is worrying me and that is this international campaign, campaign at the international level in connection with alleged or, rather, actual violations of human rights in the past few weeks. I think it is very important to prevent the creation of some kind of anti-Croatian climate or atmosphere here, and actually, I have been familiar with that for quite some time. "I know, actually" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "I know actually what all was going on behind my back here in my country in connection with my policy. In connection" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you could turn the page please, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "... with the recognition of Croatia. I would therefore like to ask you, Mr. President, and I would like to ask you explicitly for your personal engagement in connection with this first thing that I mentioned and to do something resolutely against, in other words, ensure that something is done against such criticism in connection with human rights violations. And if such criticism is justified, that you also engage personally on it. This is a matter which is very important, and I would gladly help you on that. This campaign must not succeed. An impression must not be created in the forthcoming negotiations, within the framework of the forthcoming negotiations, that Croatia actually does not wish to take on the obligation, or rather, does not wish to observe all the provisions of human rights." President Tudjman responds: "Mr. Chancellor, as you yourself have said, the reasons for that campaign are known. They are all those who are disinclined to Croatia. It goes without saying that there were certain incidents over that, but not on the part of the Croatian Army or official organs, you understand. I had 400.000 Croats expelled, from those areas which have now been liberated, 120.000. Therefore, the bitterness of these people following the liberation, following the departure of the army, could not be restrained here and there. As you can see, dear Chancellor, Ghali's report in the United Nations is more objective already. Mr. Granic, we will go back to the report of the Secretary General that President Tudjman references, but let me continue. Chancellor Kohl then says: "Once again, Mr. President, I understand that quite well. However, as a German, on the basis of my own experience, I know how it is with international campaigns, and, unfortunately, I had to realise that there was no benefit for me getting angry." Now, let's stop there because we're running short on time, Mr. Granic. But you were someone, obviously, who was a very close advisor to President Tudjman. You had a lot of experience were foreign diplomats and politicians. And let me ask you what -- when Chancellor Kohl refers to a campaign and that campaign must not succeed and then connects this with the issue of further negotiations, is this related to your comments already about the strategic goals, and can you explain how you would understand what Chancellor Kohl was warning President Tudjman about with respect to a campaign and its impact on future negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conversation and the attitudes of Chancellor Kohl were also the attitudes of a sincere friend of Croatia who warned about certain developments he had heard about and this campaign because he told me -- Mr. Kinkel told me at least 50 times that whatever happened in Croatia, great -- blame Germany for it. Was Germany the country that too early supported the international recognition of Croatia, which happened practically after the war ended? In other words, this correctly reflected the situation at the time, which means Croatia was about to begin negotiations about the peaceful reintegration of the Danube basin and also the final resolution in Bosnia-Herzegovina was something that we were waiting for and Croatia was to be an important factor there. It was difficult to achieve peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina without Croatia, and that was the main reason why Chancellor Kohl talked in this manner to President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if I understand you correctly, these allegations would have -- would have hindered or hurt the possibility of the Croatian Army then getting support to engage in military operations in Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly. Yes, that is correct. Of course, if someone is carrying out ethnic cleansing, he would not receive support for their army conducting operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Granic. Let me finish up with this page here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He says in the middle of the page in English: "I'm giving you as a friend, as a friend who feels sympathies towards your country, in your place I would actually invite some first class, serious international, that is, foreign journalists, and then I would personally talk to them, and within the framework of that discussion, I would speak very openly, completely openly, about the problems which you mentioned also, that means about the psychological situation but also your resolve to represent the position that human rights must be respected. Think about my proposal, and if you decide that you are going to do this, do it very soon because that is very good for the reputation of your country." The president says: "I will do something in that direction." And then he continues on after a comment by Mr. Kohl: "I was already intending I will speak tomorrow on the Zagreb-Split journey. I will speak about that in Karlovac. Mr. Granic, you were with President Tudjman in Karlovac, and we'll take a look at that video tomorrow, but President Tudjman then, the next day in fact, did give a statement, a public statement in Karlovac on the Zagreb-Split journey condemning the burning and looting of property; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. President Tudjman gave such a statement, but the presidents also notified me in conversation about this, and I had a series of conversations when I talked openly to the media about what was happening, that meant that there was burning and looting without any doubt, and that this should be reported but that two things should be sharply divided. One category were the incidents and even crimes, individual crimes that did happen and ethnic cleansing is something else. And I know perfectly well what ethnic cleansing is and what Croatia had gone through during four years of occupation and what was the planned and instigated departure of the Serbian population which either did not recognise the -- the Croatian state or left because of fear and because they had participated in the rebellion and had committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender 65 ter 4606.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1816.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. I'm addressing the Markac Defence. Is there any need for further conversations with the witness in relation to late released ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will address that. Yes, there is, and it will probably take less than an hour. And that would be the last session, unless we get another disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, I'd like to give you the same instruction as I did yesterday, that is, that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony already given or still to be given with one exception that you may speak to the Markac Defence about documents they have received at a very late stage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will strictly adhere to your instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the Markac Defence knows already that it is under an order, as I said yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: By all means, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in order to avoid that I will be -- that this Chamber will be put to the record as being the cause of the delay for other Chambers, we now immediately adjourn and resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 19th of November, 9.00, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 19th day of November, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
